newsitem.title: USA: Freeway destroyed by San Francisco quake is reborn.
newsitem.headline: Freeway destroyed by San Francisco quake is reborn.

text.p: A new freeway rose on Wednesday from the ruins of a double-decker highway that collapsed in a massive San Francisco earthquake eight years ago, crushing 42 motorists during the evening rush-hour.

The 4.5-mile (7.2-km) stretch of roadway opened to cars and trucks in time for the morning commute, replacing part of the Cypress Freeway that gave way during the 7.1-magnitude Loma Prieta earthquake on Oct. 17, 1989.
The collapsed freeway was the most enduring image of the 1989 quake and killed almost two-thirds of the 67 victims of the disaster.
The new single-deck structure was opened without ceremony or ribbon-cutting. "We wanted to show sensitivity to those who died in the structure," Surlene Grant, a project spokeswoman, said.
The project connects Interstate 880 to the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge toll plaza. A second and final component of the project should be completed by fall 1998, state highway officials said.
"They (commuters) seem to be very appreciative that it is open," Grant said. "It should make it easier for people to get to and from work."
Construction of the Cypress replacement project began in early 1994. The structure cost an estimated $1 billion, making it the most expensive highway project for its size in California history.

Officials said the cost was far higher than the original estimate because the state had to clean up polluted areas and settle lawsuits. The project took so long because of disputes over the freeway's route and its environmental impact.

In October 1989, the Cypress Freeway became a terrifying reminder of the destructive power of earthquakes. Pictures of the mangled wreckage were beamed around the world, becoming a symbol of the devastation wrought by the quake, which injured 3,800 people and caused $6 billion of damage.

State officials say the new Cypress structure was designed to withstand up to an 8.5-magnitude earthquake. "It's been built with all the latest seismic technology. It's a state-of-the-art freeway," Grant said.
Once completed, the freeway section is expected to carry about 116,000 cars a day and ease traffic on other San Francisco area freeways.
